prompt: Match each Carcará requirement to its kind.
hint: What, how well, or already decided by somebody else.

pairs.left: a passenger can cancel up to three hours before departure
a scan is checked in under a second with no signal

prompt: When is a requirement architecturally significant?
hint: Would meeting it, or changing it later, move the structure?

choices.text: When the business marks it as high priority
choices.why: A high-priority change to an e-mail template is still a template change.

choices.text: When it would change the structure
choices.why: Right: where data lives, what talks to what, what runs where.

choices.text: When it is a quality attribute rather than a function
choices.why: Many quality requirements are local, and some functional ones reshape the system.

choices.text: When it appears in a contract with a customer
choices.why: Contracts make requirements binding, not structural.

prompt: In the use case for cancelling a ticket, where does the lesson say the value lies?
hint: The main scenario is what everybody already imagined.

choices.text: In the main success scenario, which lists the steps
choices.why: Those steps were already in everyone's head; they rarely surprise.

choices.text: In the extensions
choices.why: Yes: each extension is a question somebody has to answer, and the answer is a requirement.

choices.text: In the precondition, which says who may cancel
choices.why: Useful, and still not where the hidden requirements were found.

choices.text: In the primary actor, which names the passenger
choices.why: It names who wants the goal; it does not discover anything new.

prompt: Put the parts of an acceptance criterion in the Given / When / Then order.
hint: A starting state, an event, the results.
items: Given a Paid ticket departing in 5 hours
And a full refund is requested once
trap: Starting with the result hides the state it depends on.

prompt: Passengers can manage their tickets. What does the lesson call this?
hint: Can anybody check it was done?

choices.text: A topic, not a requirement
choices.why: Right: nothing in it can be checked; the use case text turns it into requirements.

choices.text: A well-formed user story
choices.why: A story names the actor, the goal and the reason, and comes with criteria.

choices.text: A quality attribute
choices.why: It says nothing about how well; it is a vague function.

choices.text: A constraint from the business
choices.why: A constraint is a decision already made, such as a law or a fixed system.

prompt: Which of these are among the nine characteristics of ISO/IEC 25010:2023? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two were renamed in 2023 and one was added.

choices.text: Interaction capability
choices.why: Yes: the 2023 name for what 2011 called usability.

choices.text: Safety
choices.why: Yes: added in 2023.

choices.text: Scalability
choices.why: A common word, but not one of the nine; it lives under performance efficiency and flexibility.

choices.text: Flexibility
choices.why: Yes: the 2023 name for what 2011 called portability.

prompt: A requirements document says: The system shall be maintainable, portable and secure. What is wrong, by the lesson?
hint: A checklist copied is not a requirement.

choices.text: It uses the 2011 names
choices.why: Old names are understood; the problem is that the sentence constrains nothing.

choices.text: It lists too few characteristics
choices.why: More headings would constrain nothing either.

choices.text: It names headings without situations or numbers
choices.why: Yes: each needs to become scenarios before anybody could check it.

choices.text: Security is not a quality attribute
choices.why: It is one of the nine.

prompt: This is the boarding scenario drawn without its words. Put each part's name in its place.
hint: The dashed line surrounds the thing being stimulated.

prompt: Why does QS-02 not mention a local SQLite database on the phone?
hint: What versus how.

choices.text: Because SQLite is a constraint, not a requirement
choices.why: Nobody imposed SQLite; it is one possible design.

choices.text: Because an ISO rule keeps technology out of scenarios
choices.why: No such rule; the reason is to leave the design open and arguable.

choices.text: That is the design, which goes in a record
choices.why: Right: a scenario says what must be true, not how to make it true.

choices.text: Because the phones do not use SQLite
choices.why: They do, per lesson 2; that still does not belong in the requirement.

prompt: Which of these is the strongest quality scenario?
hint: Environment, number, scope, and it could fail.

choices.text: The ticketing API is fast and scales at peak
choices.why: No number, no situation: it cannot fail.

choices.text: Response time is optimised throughout
choices.why: A direction, not a requirement.

choices.text: 95% of purchases under 2 s at 2,000 a minute
choices.why: Yes: a situation, a measure with a scope, and a load test could prove it false.

choices.text: Average response time is under 2 seconds
choices.why: An average hides the slow tail, and there is no load in it.

prompt: In a utility tree's rating (importance, difficulty), who makes each call?
hint: One belongs to the business, one to the architect.

choices.text: The architect rates both, to keep them consistent
choices.why: Importance is a business judgement; the architect cannot make it alone.

choices.text: Each side rates the scale it knows
choices.why: Right: importance is the business's call and difficulty is the architect's, so each side rates what it knows.

choices.text: The business rates both, since it pays
choices.why: Difficulty depends on the design, which the business cannot judge.

choices.text: A vote of the whole team
choices.why: The lesson assigns each scale to whoever owns that knowledge.

prompt: Match each rating to what it means for design effort.
hint: (H, H) drives the architecture.

pairs.right: design for it, then move on
question whether to do it at all

prompt: Every leaf in a team's utility tree is rated (H, H). What should the architect do?
hint: What has the business not done?

choices.text: Start designing for each of them
choices.why: Designing for everything as top priority means no trade-off is ever decided.

choices.text: Send it back: nothing has been ranked
choices.why: Yes: the tree's job is to force a ranking on paper.

choices.text: Lower the difficulty ratings
choices.why: Difficulty is the architect's honest estimate, not a lever.

choices.text: Add more attributes to spread the ratings
choices.why: The problem is the ranking, not the number of branches.

prompt: Match each Carcará scenario to the tactic the lesson uses for it.
hint: Offline, peak, a new payment method.

prompt: A driver's phone syncs every 15 minutes during a ten-hour day. How many times does it sync?
hint: Minutes in the day divided by the interval.

prompt: Celeste chose a 15-minute sync. What did she accept?
hint: Read the line that rises with the interval.

choices.text: Drivers' phones syncing 120 times a day
choices.why: That is the 5-minute option.

choices.text: Boarding stopping when there is no signal
choices.why: Offline boarding keeps working; that is QS-02.

choices.text: A recently cancelled ticket still boards
choices.why: Yes: a ticket cancelled in the last quarter of an hour is still on the phone's list, a cost named in the decision record.

choices.text: Cancelled tickets being refunded late
choices.why: The sync affects the door, not the refund.

prompt: Put the links of the offline-boarding chain in order, from requirement to proof.
hint: Each refers to the one before by id.
items: the boarding app and sync on the deployment view
trap: A test with no requirement behind it cannot say what it protects.

prompt: Which gaps does reading a traceability matrix expose? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look for empty cells in each direction.

choices.text: A requirement no decision addresses
choices.why: Yes: nobody has designed for it.

choices.text: A decision serving no requirement
choices.why: Yes: either a requirement nobody wrote, or a removal candidate.

choices.text: A requirement nothing verifies
choices.why: Yes: a hope rather than a requirement.

choices.text: A decision written in the wrong template
choices.why: The matrix shows links, not formats.

prompt: Offline boarding and refusing cancelled tickets within a minute pull against each other. Who decides between them, and how?
hint: It is not a feature question.

choices.text: The Boarding team, by choosing a sync library
choices.why: The library implements whatever is decided; it does not decide the trade.

choices.text: The architect, by picking the stricter one
choices.why: The architect makes the costs visible; the trade-off is a business call.

choices.text: Celeste, with both costs in front of her
choices.why: Yes: the architect puts the costs on one page; the business chooses.

choices.text: Neither; a faster network meets both
choices.why: The road has no signal, which is the whole point of QS-02.

prompt: In the six-part form, the part that holds the number, such as within one second for every scan, is the response ___.
hint: How anybody knows the response was good enough.
